revisions.body: The older accusations matter because they reach the jury before the courtroom does. Socrates says that many listeners encountered the story of him in childhood, when they were especially ready to believe it, and that this story portrayed him as a thinker about the heavens and the underworld who could make a weaker argument seem stronger. He also says that most of these accusers cannot be summoned or questioned. One way to read his strategy, then, is as a struggle over the jury’s starting point: before they assess the present indictment, he tries to loosen an inherited picture of who he is.

Here Socrates diagnoses a gap between accusation and specification: when asked what he does or teaches, the hostile voices, as he portrays them, have no answer and fall back on familiar accusations against philosophers. Read this as his rhetorical analysis of the rumor, not as evidence that the later formal indictment uses those words. The force of the move lies in shifting attention from lurid labels to the missing account of his actual practice.

Socrates recasts the penalty as a measure of civic benefit. The man who urges citizens to care for their goodness and wisdom, he says, needs leisure; free meals in the Prytaneum would therefore fit the service he claims to offer. His comparison with the Olympic victor sharpens the point: athletic success makes the city seem happy, while his work aims at happiness itself. One cautious reading is that he is proposing his own measure of civic worth; whether the proposal follows an established procedure is not assessed here.

The proposal creates a genuine interpretive fork. Socrates presents free meals in the Prytaneum as fitting the civic benefit he claims, but the accepted record treats the proposal as a counter-penalty and leaves its seriousness unassessed. What should guide your hearing: his confidence in the value of his service, the provocation of naming such a reward, or a mixture of both? The passage gives room for those readings without requiring us to choose one as settled fact.

Socrates’ refusal to propose a penalty he regards as harmful sets the test for the alternatives that follow. Exile, in particular, is not presented as a neutral escape: he argues that other citizens would respond to his conversations much as Athenians have, and sketches two routes by which expulsion could follow—through the young who listen or through their older relatives. The point is not that exile is proven impossible, but that, on Socrates’ reasoning, it would not preserve the way of life he is defending.

One way to hear this turn is as a change in the courtroom’s direction. Socrates is no longer defending himself; he makes the condemners answerable to a future generation of examiners. The prophecy therefore does more than forecast punishment: it relocates the pressure of examination beyond the verdict. The judges may close this trial, but not the question of how they live.

Socrates offers the judges an argument from silence. His divine sign, which he says often stopped him over small matters, did not oppose him at home, on the way to court, or during the speech. From that absence he infers that what has happened, including his coming death, is likely good. The inference depends on the premise that the sign would have warned him before harm; the record preserves Socrates’ reasoning without confirming that premise. The striking feature is the weight he places on a silence.

revisions.title: The last appeal to the jurors
revisions.body: At the close, Socrates joins consolation to a final appeal. He presents death as no harm to a good man, then asks the jurors—not Athens in the abstract—to correct his sons if they prize money or anything else above virtue, or mistake self-importance for worth. He leaves the final judgment with the god: he will die, they will live, and the better lot remains unknown.
